en: The Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Heshan Chaogongfang.
When the Master first took up residence at Longqing, he ascended the hall to offer incense.

Having finished offering prayers for the longevity of the Emperor, he next held up the incense and said: "This one portion of incense is offered in honor of my predecessor who resided at Mount Huanglong as the tenth [abbot]."
The Second Generation: Chan Master Xin. He burned incense in the burner and said, "I shall twist the nostrils of the patch-robed monks throughout the world.
Thereupon, he sat cross-legged. The presiding monk struck the gavel and said, "In this Dharma assembly, you dragon-like and elephant-like multitudes should contemplate the primary principle.

The Master looked at the great assembly and said, "A single stick of agalloch and sandalwood incense wondrously enters the spirit; the Chan path, looking northward from the Yellow River, has already opened its ferry-crossing. From afar, it is praised as the sun beneath heaven."
"May you live as long as a mountain; I pray that you may emulate Hua Feng in offering blessings to the Sage. "Is there no one among the assembly who will take up the refrain?
At that time, a monk stepped forward and asked, "The Dharma that the Tathāgata could not fully exhaust in forty-nine years—today I request the Master to speak of it.
The Master said, "Zha! The monk said, "The public case that Bodhidharma did not resolve in nine years—today..."
"I hope the Master will bring this out. The Master said, "Ten-thousand-mile divine light, the mark behind the crown.

The monk said, "As for the ancients seeking stillness amidst bustle and seeking bustle within stillness—did they benefit people while in the midst of bustle, or did they benefit people while in stillness?
The Master said, "Cut off both ends; return home and sit securely. The monk said, "If that is so, then Longshan..."

"I have clearly attained the Zen of the Patriarchs; the Dharma has been transmitted this very morning at the moment of its raising. The Master said, "The Dharma is fundamentally without transmission. How then do you transmit it?
The monk said, "In the past, I personally received the essential meaning on the mountain peak; today I bring it forth so that all quarters may know.
The Master said, "Repeated words should not be swallowed."
The Master then said: "If we discuss the primary truth (*paramārtha-satya*), even before the mallet has been struck, it has already been manifestly revealed in its full majesty.
Why is this? Furthermore, the wondrous Way of all Buddhas is pure and inherently so; its measure encompasses the great void.

All things with sentience and those without sentience, form and emptiness, light and darkness—all share one and the same essence-nature. Since they share one and the same essence, what is that nature?"

The physical forms they receive are each different; this is truly because a single thought momentarily arises as emotional dust, which, in conjunction with the illusory shadows of the six sense objects such as form and sound, gives rise to false attachments.

Suddenly, when a single thought turns its light inward, the mind’s eye opens wide, and one immediately perceives the empty space of the ten directions and the great assembly before them—whether appearing in the bodies of officials or in the guise of bhikṣus—all of whom are but one.

The time for its manifestation has arrived. It is like a single ingot of pure gold fashioned into various different objects; though their forms differ, the nature of the gold itself is fundamentally one.
Even if you were to perceive this with such clarity and distinctness, you would still not yet possess the skillful means to transcend Vairocana and surpass Śākyamuni.
Have you not seen how, in the past at the assembly on Vulture Peak, the World-Honored One held up a flower before a multitude of hundreds of thousands of people?
[The Buddha] held up a flower and showed it to the great assembly. Among those present, only Mahākāśyapa smiled.
The World-Honored One then said, "I possess the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye, the wondrous mind of Nirvāṇa, the reality-phenomenon which is without characteristics; I entrust this to Mahākāśyapa.

This is the separate transmission outside the teachings, pointing directly at the human mind so that one may see one's nature and become a Buddha. Regarding this causal connection, the discussion among the assembly is most intense.
Some say: "Kāśyapa has already lost his head at the very beginning. Others say: "Everyone sees it clearly;
it is simply that they are unwilling to accept it. Still others say: "Why not realize it before the flower was even held up?
Such understandings as these are all the result of twisting and manipulating the faculty of thought, forcibly engaging in conjecture; none of them know the definitive point. If one were to know it...

Truly so! The imperial grace and the Buddha’s grace are both fully repaid at once. Should this not yet be so, today before this great assembly of humans and devas, I shall settle the matter all at once.
He then raises his whisk and says: "Look, look! Tell me, how far is this from Vulture Peak? After a long silence, he says:
"Thoroughly transcending the three periods of time, the wondrous; discussing the mind, it fully repays the kindness of the One Man."
Ascending the hall, he said: "Time passes in an instant; it is already the eighth day.

Those who practice Zen must act as if their hair were on fire—do not wait until the light from your eyes falls to the ground, for by then it will be too late to regret. To come back after passing through the 'unobstructed' state of death is a swift process, yet twenty years have passed.
This is why those of the Two Vehicles do not comprehend all phenomena and realize only a single emptiness."

[If one clings to] principle, it results in annihilationism. When a Bodhisattva person realizes the principle of the single emptiness (*ekāśūnyatā*), they comprehend all phenomena (*sarvadharma*) such that annihilationism does not arise.
Thus, one knows that while nothing exists [independently], all phenomena manifest before one. It is not seen that [this contradicts] the monk’s question to Master Tianpeng:
"What is the Buddha? Tianpeng said: "Intimate and never leaving home; silent and never facing the door. The Master said: "Tianpeng..."
To speak in such a manner ultimately results in leakage. Tell me, among the three kinds of leakage, into which one does this fall?
Do you wish to understand? "Without body but with affairs, one transcends the diverging paths; Without affairs and without body, one falls into the beginning and the end."
Ascending the hall, he raised the example of Master Xinghua. One day, seeing the rector Kebin, he said, "Before long, you shall become a master of the liturgy.
Kebin replied, "I will not enter this protective community. Xinghua said, "Do you refuse to enter because you have already understood?"
[The monk] said, "I will not enter. Kebin said, "Even if you try to evade it, there is no connection [between us]. Xinghua said, "Kebin, the Rector, has been defeated in the battle of Dharma.

He shall be fined five strings of cash and provide a meal of *kai* rice. The following day at the time of the midday meal, he himself struck the gavel and said, "Kebin, the Rector, was defeated in the battle of Dharma.
He has been fined five strings of cash and must provide a hall of *kai* rice; furthermore, he is not permitted to eat it."
After the meal, he left the hall. Later, his Dharma heir was Xinghua. The Master said, "Venerable Kebin was truly like a cliff rising ten thousand fathoms high.
Although he understood how to go in such a manner, he had not yet mastered the faculty of discerning the capacities of beings. The old man Xinghua was not only able to sail with the wind;
he could also steer against the wind. Tell me, was it because he was defeated in a battle of Dharma that he became his successor?"
Xinghua: Here is a phrase that is well able to effect the mutual exchange of self and others. Is there anyone who can speak it?
If not, today I cannot help but briefly open a single thread. Who would have known that on the ninth day of the ninth month, the eighth was already the Double Ninth Festival?
Master Xie Hua ascends the hall. He cites: One day the World-Honored One ordered Ānanda to carry his bowl. Ānanda responded with an "Amen" and set forth.
The World-Honored One said, "Since you are carrying the bowl, you must follow the ritual of the seven Buddhas of the past. Ānanda then asked:
"What is the ritual of the seven Buddhas of the past? The World-Honored One called to Ānanda, and Ānanda responded.
The World-Honored One said, "Take this bowl and go. The Master said: "Ānanda only knew how to go like that; he did not know how to come back like that.
The Layman of Longqing, however, knows both how to go like that and how to come back like that. Even so, tell me, what do you say?"

This is the ritual of the Seven Buddhas. Do you understand? A man of spirit naturally possesses the will to pierce the heavens; he does not walk where the Tathāgata has walked. Entering the hall, he said:
"The three dots of the circle have not yet been lightly repaid; when every phrase is free from self-interest, one may simply rest. The point of the tip—"
To attempt to deliberate upon it with the intellect is futile; its luminous clarity is fundamentally not something that can be confronted head-on.
If one lets go, there are tracks leading every which way; if one holds fast, it is as impenetrable as a sealed door. Within this lies a single stroke that falls into neither extreme.

Even if one manages to reach such a state, it is still merely following a pattern and looking through holes to drive wedges. For such a person, throughout the twelve periods of the day, there is always something hidden within the breast.
All of these are matters pertaining to the shores of birth and death. If you wish to pass through the secure barrier, you must pull out the wedge from behind your head.

Entering the hall, he said: "Every day, whether you are sitting quietly in the hall or walking for alms in the marketplace—whether you look in quiet places or look in noisy places—you should know that this matter is never interrupted at any time or place."

Seeing that Master Xuefeng addressed the assembly, saying: "If one were to take up the entire earth and reduce it to the size of a grain of millet, and cast it before you—yet the 'lacquer buckets' do not understand;
beat the drum for a communal viewing! The Master said: "Lingqiong does not even need to beat the drum."
Simply look in this manner. Even if you do not yet see through it, it will nonetheless serve as the cultivation of seeds of goodness.
Should you suddenly manage to see through it, you will finally know that Master Longqing’s heart was one of urgent compassion.
Nevertheless, even so, thirty years from now, do not fail the mountain monk.
Ascending the hall, [the Master] raised this case: On the road to Mount Tai there was an old woman.

Whenever a monk asked her, "Which way goes to Mount Tai? the woman would say, "Go straight ahead. As soon as the monk had walked three or five paces, the woman would say, "What a fine monk, yet you go like that!
Later, another monk related this to Zhaozhou. Zhaozhou said, "Wait; I shall go to examine this woman for him."
The old woman said, "Tomorrow I shall go. He questioned her again in the same manner, and she answered him in the same manner.
When Zhaozhou returned, he said to the assembly, "I have thoroughly investigated and exposed the old woman of Mount Tai. The Master said: "One person distinguishes the field by its sprouts;
another does not tremble when facing a precipice. Do you all wish to recognize Zhaozhou? After a long silence, he said: 'A tiger in the midst of a bustling market.'"
Ascending the hall on the day of the Start of Spring, he said: "The ritual tubes blow out the ash at this very hour; one should recognize and perceive the person who tends the ox.
Having plowed the field of the mind until not a single patch remains, one must believe that the numinous sprout does not violate the spring. Thus, there is growth in spring and falling in autumn."

Flowers bloom before the eyes of those with cataracts; they do not fall through the process of change. The spiritual mechanism is revealed alone; the four seasons cannot alter it, and ten thousand transformations cannot displace it.
Even one with an iron forehead and copper eyes—who would dare look directly at its head? Nevertheless, even so, this is still the full manifestation of the true command.
But as for the phrase "Receiving blessings in accordance with the time"—how about that? After a long silence, he said: "Just..."
Having obtained the clay ox to plow the ridges and furrows, what need is there for a jade tablet worn at the waist?
Ascending the hall, he said: "First function, then illumination—this is required to test a master. First illumination, then function—no trace remains.

Illumination and function simultaneous—standing like a wall a thousand fathoms high. Illumination and function not simultaneous—the sense bases and objects may be clearly reflected. The ancients used this...
The four turning phrases are used to test the monks of the world. Unless one possesses the true eye and has attained intimate, clear realization, it is difficult to find a foothold here.
Today, for the sake of you all, I have clearly brought them forth. Do you understand?

If you do understand, you may be said to have transcended the ground of awakening instantly, without moving so much as a hair’s breadth. If this is not yet the case, you must apply yourself with utmost diligence.
It is subtle. For this reason, when the ancients encountered a single turning of the causal conditions, they were immediately unable to rest even in sleep or food.
You brothers today see it as something trivial; while you are still physically secure and your strength is robust, you must quickly realize it.
Do not wait until the day your eyes fall from their sockets. At such a time, do not say that Elder Longqing did not tell you.
Ascending the hall, [the Master] raised the following case: One day while sitting with Layman Pang, Songshan picked up a ruler and asked the Layman, "Do you see it?
The Layman said, "I see it. Songshan said, "What do you see? The Layman said, "Songshan. Songshan said, "..."
"You must not speak of it. The Master said, "How could I not speak of it? Yunmen then threw down his measuring rule. The Master said, "To have a head but no tail invites people's resentment.
Yunmen said, "Were it not for this old fellow, one would not even get that far. The Master said, "In what way does he fail to get there?
Yunmen said, "At the point where there is a head but no tail. The Master said, "It is permissible to gain the weak from among the strong; but from among the weak—"
As soon as [Pang] gained the upper hand, the Master seized him. The Layman said, "Among them all, this old fellow has no way to hold a conversation.
The Master said, "Layman Pang’s lifelong eloquence was unstoppable; had it not been for Songshan, he would have surely been knocked down by the second level of response."

Ascending the hall, the Master raised the case: Panshan said, "When light and its objects are both forgotten, what is it? Dongshan said, "While light and its objects have not yet been forgotten, what is it?
The Master said: "The mountains, rivers, and the great earth; the lanterns and the pillars; the kitchen, the storehouse, and the three gates—all these are light and its objects.
What, then, is the reality? You all wander through the three realms precisely because you do not understand."
The present dharma proceeds from birth until death without end; you must quickly realize it.
Do not wait until your hair is white and your beard silver, like digging a well when thirsty—by then, regret will come too late.

Ascending the hall, the Master raised an example: One day, when Linji was carrying his alms bowl to a householder’s home and said, "Please fill my bowl," an old woman came to the door and said, "How insatiable you are!
Linji replied, "I have not even dreamed of the food; why do you say I am so insatiable?
Thereupon, the old woman shut the door. The Master said, "Everyone says that Linji fell into the hands of this old woman."
A pitfall. Yet those who have not experienced bitter hardship do not know it. What they fail to realize is that where the door is shut, the precious treasure is already revealed.
I dare ask all of you: since the door has been shut, where is the precious treasure? After a long silence, he said: "Press! (Za).
The Assembly of Five Hundred Arhats. Entering the hall in the evening, he said: "Today there has been such great clamor;
where has it all gone? Each of you should observe clearly: all dharmas are exactly like this. Therefore, the ancients had many skillful means for the sake of others.
It is just as they say: 'When facing the wind, do not face the seal. This means that one must be fully pervasive in every encounter. When facing the seal..."

It does not accord with the wind. Yet, how can it be helped that its literary brilliance has already been manifested? To discern the mark along the universal path, one must avoid striking against the sharp edge [of conceptualization].
When the way harmonizes with the source, it directly subdues all views.

Have you not seen how, in the past, at the assembly of Lingjian, five hundred bhikṣus attained the four dhyānas and acquired the supernormal power of recollecting past lives; each of them beheld for themselves their past relinquishing of bodies and taking up of new bodies?
"Killing one's father, harming one's mother, killing an Arhat, shedding the blood of a Buddha—these various grave offenses cause one to feel fear and dread.
Thereupon, Mañjuśrī, brandishing a sword, threatened Gautama. Gautama said, "Stop! Stop!
You must not commit such a heinous act. Do not seek to harm me. If I am to be harmed, let it be for the sake of goodness. Mañjuśrī, all dharmas arise from..."
From the very beginning, there has been no self or person. When one perceives a self or person within the inner mind, and when that inner mind arises, the "self" is inevitably harmed;
this is precisely what is meant by "harm. At that moment, five hundred bhikṣus each awakened to their own original mind and praised him in unison, saying:
"Mañjuśrī, the Great Sage of Wisdom, who has profoundly penetrated the source and depths of the Dharma, personally grasps a sharp sword and holds it to [the throat] as if..."
The coming body is like a sword; the Buddha is also thus. One mark, without duality; no marks, nothing produced.
Within this, how could there be killing? The Master said: "The old fellow Mañjuśrī can truly be called one who pulls out the wedge and extracts the nail.
Even if five hundred bhikṣus were to attain enlightenment all at once, it would still be the same pit with no different soil. *Chán*.
Ascending the hall, the Master raised an ancient case: A monk asked Dàlóng, “The physical body decays; what is the pure *dharmakāya*?

Dàlóng replied, “Mountain flowers bloom like brocade; stream water is as clear as indigo. The Master said, “This monk had only the moon reflecting on the wall, but lacked the wind blowing through the leaves.
Had it not been for Dàlóng’s total exertion of his faculties, the matter would have nearly been split into two parts. Study!”
Ascending the hall, he raised the case of Caoshan Huichao, who said: "To act as a water buffalo is to fall into conformity with categories. The Master added his own comment:
"Being within a category, how could one ever be equal to that category? "To not accept food twice is to fall into nobility.

The Master added his own comment: "If you recognize it, you are already unfit. "Not severing sound and form is to fall everywhere. The Master added his own comment: "You must penetrate through directly."
Passing before the skull, these three words constitute a shortcut for entering the Way. One must clearly perceive the point where the path begins so that one does not go astray.
Even if you perceive this with such bold clarity, it remains merely a painted image;
whether shallow or deep, you must personally arrive there once before it is attained. How can one personally arrive? After a long silence...
It is said: "Not falling into the realm of merit and achievement, exhausting the very act of seeing; far transcending shadow and echo, penetrating directly to the heart of mind.
At the opening of the summer retreat, there was a small *can* (private instruction). [The Master] raised the case of the Venerable Tianping Congyi, who went to Xiyuan.

He often said of himself, "Do not speak of 'understanding the Buddha-dharma'; nowadays, one cannot even find a person capable of raising a *hua-tou* (critical phrase). Xiyuan knew this. One day, seeing him from afar, he [said]:
Xiyuan summoned Congyi. Congyi raised his head. Xiyuan said, "Wrong. After Congyi had walked two or three steps, Xiyuan said again, "Wrong.
Congyi stepped forward once more. Xiyuan asked, "As for those two 'wrongs' just now, was it Xiyuan who was wrong, or was it you, the Senior Monk?
Congyi said, "It was I, Congyi, who was wrong. Xiyuan said, "Wrong, wrong! Congyi withdrew, and Xiyuan said, "Stay right here for a moment."
After the summer retreat, he waited to discuss these two errors with the Senior Seat Holder (Upādhyāya). At that time, Yiqi departed immediately.
After taking up residence at the monastery, he said to the assembly: "When I first went on pilgrimage, I was blown by the winds of karma to the place of Elder Ximing.
He gave me two consecutive blows [of the staff] and further asked me to stay for the summer retreat to discuss them with him. I do not say that it was an error at such a time."
Setting out for the south, he already knew it was a mistake. Later, Shoushan said, "Based on Tianping’s interpretation, you have not even dreamed of Xiyuan.
Why is this so? The Master said, "Fromyi once displayed his brilliance."
Alas, how regrettable that he has fallen into the trap of West Monastery! Little did he know that West Monastery possesses the skillful means to pull out nails and extract wedges.
Nevertheless, as the saying goes: "If the bitter gourd is bitter at the root, the sweet melon is sweet to the core."
Record of the Relocation and Installation at He Shan.
Ascending the Seat, he said: "If you wish to understand the phrase for entering the gate, it has been entrusted to you even before a word is spoken. Apply your full effort directly here."
"There is no need for mutual interplay. Is there anyone among you who is sharp and brilliant? Come forth and speak! (The questions and answers are not recorded).
The Master then said: "Before Daxi, the true mechanism was revealed alone; with Chengyuan reaching this point, the Patriarchal Command has flourished once more.
Why labor over the four questions? It is simply a matter of sitting in meditation. There is no need to pluck at leaves or seek out branches; one must transcend directly."
The Buddha transcends the patriarchs; how could this be a matter of borrowing function to clarify status? It is entirely because they harmonize with the subtle and penetrate the source.
If you wish to thoroughly understand the Three Mysteries, look at the very first phrase. Then, taking his whisk, he drew a diagram and said, "Look!"
Ascending the hall, [the Master] raised the following case: Bodhidharma said to the Second Patriarch, "You need only externally cease all conditions and internally let the mind be without panting;
with a mind like a wall, you may enter the Way. The Second Patriarch explained various principles concerning mind and nature, yet none of them accorded with the truth.
One day, he suddenly attained great enlightenment and said to Bodhidharma, "From this point forward, I can rest all conditions. Bodhi...
Dharma said, "Is it not a falling into annihilation? The Patriarch replied, "No. Dharma asked, "How is it, my son?
The Patriarch said, "It is clearly and eternally known; it cannot be expressed in words. Dharma said, "This is what has been transmitted by all the Buddhas; do not harbor any further doubt."
The Master said: "If the mind is like a wall, why is it that it knows clearly and constantly?

If you can see it thus, you may be said to eat all day long without ever having bitten through a single grain of rice. It would be such that the empty space of the ten directions would entirely dissolve away.
If this is not yet so, then the consciousness of karma will be in a frantic rush, wandering through the three miserable realms with no end in sight. Investigate!"
Ascending the hall, he said: "Turning my head, I see that time passes like a whirling tumbleweed; look, the nine months of summer are drawing to a close.
You must quickly awaken to the phrase within the mystery; do not labor in vain by chasing after the dust of worldly emotions. What is the phrase within the mystery? Do you wish to understand?"
The first mystery: profound and deep, it directly illuminates the era before Vimalakīrti. The second mystery: although the question and answer transcend verbal expression. The third mystery:
a single phrase according to capacity is inherently without partiality. Therefore, the ancients said:

"Every utterance must embody the three mysteries and the three essentials. If they do not embody the three mysteries and the three essentials, they are all merely common, worldly teachers. These three...
These phrases and words serve to test the eyes of those who study under a master. Whether one has attained awakening and clarity can be verified by this;
whether one has transcended the three realms can likewise be verified by this. You must realize this quickly; do not wait until you are once again entangled in the suffering of illness.
The path ahead is bustling; there is no time for regret. [The Master] descends from his seat. He ascends the hall and cites a case:
A monk asked the Venerable Heshan of old, “What is the Way? Heshan said, “When the farmer tills the field, he does not return home.
The monk asked, “What is one who is on the Way? Heshan said, “When the grain ripens, he does not go to the market. Later, Shoushan...
He uttered these two phrases: "The field-plougher does not return home. What is the meaning? Shanshan said, "Great merit is not rewarded with a banner.
What is "the grain ripens but one does not go to the field"? Shoushan said, "Let it rot from wind and rain.
The Master said, "Old man Heyang can truly be said to have penetrated the subtle and entered the profound; his golden needle has double locks. Although Master Shoushan, based on..."

He acted accordingly. Yet, how could it be that every word of his did not accord with the Way? Even so, this was still the teaching of Gushan. In a small-scale sermon (*xiaocan*), he cited Nan-yuan’s address to the assembly, which said:
"People everywhere possess only the eye for the simultaneous act of pecking and hatching, but they do not possess the function of the simultaneous act of pecking and hatching.
At that time, a monk stepped forward and asked, "What is the function of the simultaneous act of pecking and hatching?"
The Master of the Monastery said, "A master does not wait for the pecking and the breaking; when the pecking and the breaking occur simultaneously, both are lost.
A monk said, "This has always been the point where a student asks. The Master said, "How do you act at that very point of questioning? The monk said, "Lost. The Master then struck him.

The Teacher said, "To extract the nails and pull out the wedges—one must have the skillful means of Nan-yuan to achieve this. At that time, had it not been for this monk, it would have been difficult indeed."
Difficult to sustain. Be careful.
[The Master] ascends the hall. He cites the story of Zen Master Yangshan. One day, while he was sitting in meditation, a monk crept up and stood by his side.
Yangshan opened his eyes, saw him, and then drew a circle on the ground, writing the character for "water" beneath it. He then looked toward his attendants.
A monk [approached]. The monk made no reply. The Master said, "This monk plays with danger atop a ten-thousand-fathom precipice.
Old man Yangshan, whose fame spreads across the four seas—why do you provide a redundant commentary for others? Examine!"

Ascending the hall, the Master said: "It reaches the point where everything encountered is unobstructed, and one penetrates the names, phrases, and sentences. Mountains, rivers, and the great earth are 'names,' yet even these names cannot be grasped.
This is called the complete possession of the samādhi and the ocean of nature; yet this is still like ripples swirling without wind.
You must further know that there is the simultaneous application of illumination and function according to the occasion—the single aperture of the ultimate remains. The Master then raised his whisk.
The Master said: "Look, look! To call it a whisk is to be obstructed at every turn; not to call it a whisk is likewise to be obstructed at every turn.
Even if you do not proceed in either of these ways, you are still like ripples surging in a windless sea.
If you wish to pass through the secure barrier, you must further possess the eye upon the crown of your head. What, then, is this eye upon the crowns of your heads? It is excellent.
Jiuyun said: "Within non-illumination and function, illumination and function are realized; where there is achievement, achievement is transcended.
He ascended the hall and, citing Chan Master Xiujing of Huayan, who served as the *vina* (chant master) at Luopo, remarked: "One day, he struck the gavel and said:"
He addressed the assembly: "Upstairs they are stacking firewood; downstairs they are weeding the fields. The Head Seat asked, "What is the Holy Monk doing?
The Rector said, "He does not sit upright in the hall, nor does he respond to the dual functions at either end. The Master said, "The Head Seat only understands how to come this way;
yet how can one deny that the Rector is skilled at appraising the price? Even if one examines it closely, it is still but a shadow of the body."
[The Master] said: "Do you all still want this story to be resolved? After a long silence, he said: 'Just so.
He ascended the hall and cited Xuan Sha’s address to the assembly: "Not seeing a single dharma is a great calamity. Jing Qing pointed to a pillar and asked:
"Is it that you do not see this? Xuan Sha replied: "The clear water and white rice of Zhejiang—I give them back to you."
"Consume it! As for the Buddha-dharma, you have not even dreamed of it. The Master said, "It is generally said that Xuansha’s spiritual mechanism is in his palm;
its bestowal and revocation are worth observing. If you hold such a view, where is your eye of study? You simply do not realize it."
Jingqing was a "white-handed thief. Although it is so, how can he deceive those with clear eyes?
He ascended the hall and, citing the Ancestor Master Zifu of Jizhou, addressed the assembly, saying: "The first phrase: even the Patriarchs did not know its existence."
The second phrase: capable of serving as a teacher to the patriarchs and Buddhas. The third phrase: upholding and elevating the patriarchs and Buddhas. The Master said:
"There is one phrase where you have no place to grasp; there is one phrase that seizes the life-vein of the *śramaṇa*; there is one phrase that is vividly clear.
Even if you can discern these three phrases, it is still merely the study of Buddha-dharma; it is not yet [the ultimate]."
The point of entry for awakening. Do you people wish to awaken? [He strikes the meditation seat with his whisk. He descends from the seat.
Ascending the hall, he strikes the meditation seat once with the whisk and says: "If you do not look back when it is raised, you are already mistaken; if you attempt to deliberate, you are lost."
In what kalpa will you awaken? If you see such a raising [of the staff], you do not look back; if you do not see such a raising, you likewise do not look back.
Upon reaching this point, you must transcend through both "knocking" and "singing" in order to fully repay the national debt of gratitude. If this is not yet so, [you have failed].
"I cannot help but cast a golden needle upon the summit of Mount Sumeru. After a long silence, he said: "Do you understand?
Only those who know how to see the moonlight in stillness can hear the sound of the spring from its depths."
Ascending the hall, [the Master] raised the case of Chan Master Huangbo Xiyun. While he was clearing fields at Baizhang, Baizhang said, "Dharma Brother Yun, it is no small task to clear these fields.
Huangbo replied, "I am merely performing manual labor along with the assembly. Baizhang said, "It must have been troublesome for you to serve the Way.
Huangbo replied, "How would I dare decline such toil? Baizhang asked, "How much field have you cleared? Huangbo struck the ground three times with his hoe. Baizhang—
He then shouted. Huangbo covered his ears and departed. The Master said: "Bai Zhang’s correct command was like the wind blowing over grass that bows;
Huangbo’s cultivation of the field was like water reaching a channel that forms. Although it was thus, tell me: as for the place where he struck the ground with the hoe, what was that?"
Do you understand? It is not that those who have not experienced bitter toil do not know.
Master Fazhu ascended the hall and said: "I cite the case of Layman Luoshan. When he was parting from Master Fazhu, he posed this question: 'In front of you is the Grand Councilor (Taifu).
If he were suddenly to ask the Master, "How do you instruct your disciples throughout the twelve periods of the day? how would you answer? Fazhu..."
The candidate had no reply. Luoshan said, "Just say: 'Riding the tiger's head, gathering in the tiger's tail. Under a single phrase, the fundamental principle is clarified.
He then spoke on behalf of the candidate, saying, "This is still the verbal teaching of a Bodhisattva. What about the non-verbal teaching of a Bodhisattva? The candidate again had no reply.
Luoshan further said, "Facing each other with exposed, sharp mechanisms is like a flash of lightning or a stroke of a broom. The Master said: [This is the meaning].

Throughout the monastic communities, everyone deliberated on this, saying that the transformation-monk (the teacher) had no words; yet they failed to realize that there was, in fact, a mechanism for trapping a tiger.
Luoshan regretted not having been able to hand it over with both hands. But alas, those who enter through the gate do not possess the family treasure.
Do you all wish to recognize the family treasure? After a long silence, he said: "Look for it five days from now."
Ascending the hall, the Master raised the following case: When Master Xuansha asked a monk, "What is that before you?
the monk replied, "A tiger. Xuansha said, "It is you; why do you call it a tiger? The Master said: "In this Sahā world, there are four kinds of most grave matters.
If one can penetrate them, one will undoubtedly transcend the realm of shadows and boundaries. He further said: "If you wish to recognize Xuansha’s tiger, look directly at his face."
Who is it that beholds? Directly penetrating the secure barrier, the entire mechanism transcends Buddhas and patriarchs.
*Chen* (Exertion). Entering the hall: That which is prior to the fifteenth day is the first phrase; that which is subsequent to the fifteenth day is the second phrase.
The fifteenth day of the month at the Main Hall is the third phrase. The first phrase clarifies that one has attained the ability to cut off the tongues of all people under heaven.
The second phrase clarifies that one stands forth majestically and alone. The third phrase clarifies that one’s divine blade stands like a sheer cliff.
If you can clarify these three phrases, the imperial grace and the Buddha’s grace will both be fully repaid at once. If this is not yet the case, you must apply yourself with diligence.
A single stroke transcends the manifest; wondrously identical, the three phrases enter the unconditioned.
[The Master] ascended the hall and cited the case where Grand Protector An asked Master Sanjiao, "The new year has already arrived; where has the old year gone?
Sanjiao replied, "A peach-wood talisman is nailed to the wall. The Master said, "Fushan Yuan Chan Master called these words 'the golden needle.'"
The "Double Locks. Later generations have followed the model and copied the likeness, yet they do not realize that a painted cake cannot satisfy hunger.

Grand Protector An has already missed the mark before our very eyes; had it not been for the Monk of Sanjiao, who maintained the teaching with total, vertical integrity, how could the wind have blown and the grass have bent?
Ascending the hall, [the Master] raised the following case: When Guishan asked Yangshan, "I heard that when you were at Baizhang, you would answer ten for every one asked;
is this true? Yangshan replied, "I did not dare. Guishan said, "Bring forth a single phrase that goes beyond this.

As Yangshan prepared to open his mouth, Guishan gave a shout. This happened three times; each time Yangshan prepared to speak, he was met with a shout. Thereupon, Yangshan wept and said, "The former..."
The Master said, "My teaching requires that you meet the right person before it can be realized. Today, indeed, you have met such a person.

Thereupon, he resolved his mind and tended the ox for three years. One day, while Yangshan was sitting in meditation beneath a tree, Guishan pointed to his back with a staff and asked, "Has Jizi spoken yet?
Yangshan replied, "Although I have not spoken, I certainly do not borrow [from others]."
Another person’s words. Guishan said, "Jizi understands. The Master remarked, "Guishan and Yangshan—one question and one answer—are indeed intimate and direct;
yet, fundamentally, they lack the principles of the Buddha-dharma. If one examines them closely, under Heyshan’s gate, they could only pass as mere sweepers. He then descended from his seat.
Opening the furnace, he ascended the hall. He cited the story of Chan Master Xuanzhen: Once, when Fayen, Wukong, and Longji arrived, they were warming themselves by the fire at night.
A manifested arhat appeared from the hearth and asked, "Are the mountains, rivers, and the great earth the same as, or different from, your own self, venerable masters?
Longji said, "Different. The arhat held up two fingers. Longji said, "The same. The arhat likewise held up two fingers.
The Master said, "This fellow has not even finished warming himself by the fire, yet he continues to prattle on about sameness and difference.
Even if you were to perceive them with vivid discernment, you would still be merely on the road. Under Heishan’s gate, you must simply receive a blow of the staff.
Why? Because nine out of ten words are better left as one silence."
Ascending the hall, the Master raised an ancient case: A monk asked Zen Master Qingyuan Si, "What is the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma?

Si replied, "What is the price of rice in Luling? The Master said: "Everyone says that Zen Master Si borrowed water to offer flowers, yet they fail to realize there was a discourse beyond the ordinary.
Do you wish to see the point of the Ancients' intimacy? The price of rice in Luling—past and present."

The Transmission: The events are clear and distinct; the matter is plain. If you wish to understand the essential meaning within this, wear your grandmother’s clothes and bow for your grandmother’s birthday.
Ascending the hall, he raised the example of Master Yunmen addressing the assembly: "Now it is the mid-summer retreat. At the point of impact, speak forth!"
"Bring forth a single phrase! The assembly was speechless. He said himself, "Mitraku mitraki chi.
Again he asked, "What about 'Mitraku mitraki chi'? He provided the answer himself, saying, "Bulin. Again he said, "Keppa" (a knock).
The Master said, "Master Yunmen is just like washing a clod of earth in the mud. To penetrate this and reach his gate, one must have eyebrows."
Now, entering the hall:
the weather has just turned cool. You practitioners of Zen must apply yourselves with diligence throughout the two-and-six hours of the day.
Fundamentally, in the practice of Zen, one must first have a point of entry; only then can one sit securely. Once you have attained the ability to sit securely, only then...

Only when you understand how to establish your livelihood do you have the capacity to engage in the discourse of Zen meditation; furthermore, you must know how to apply yourself to the practice of *kung-fu* before you can succeed.
Consider this: when one person departs from the source with true realization, the empty space of the ten directions entirely vanishes.
Yet, right now before our eyes, the myriad phenomena of the universe stand vividly and fully manifest. How can they be made to vanish? Some might say:
What do you call the myriad phenomena of the universe? It is also said: "Form, in its very essence, is emptiness. It is also said:
"Whatever meets the eye or encounters conditions is all illusory; ultimately, returning to the root, it is entirely the one empty substance.

It is also said: "Do not concern yourself with anything anywhere; simply remain without mind amidst the ten thousand things. What harm is there in the ten thousand things constantly surrounding you? If this is so...
Such a view fails to realize that this was the skillful means (*upāya*) of the ancients; it may be said that they were defeated before even being examined.
Therefore, the Gate of the Patriarchs has three seals: The first seal stamps the sky: the great earth is fully raised, and all points of contact are permeated.

The second seal stamps the mud: in every atom and every world-system, all appear simultaneously. The third seal stamps the water: pure illumination reflects as cold waves turn over to the very bottom. These are the three seals.
This is the Single Seal. This one seal puts all the patch-robed monks under heaven to the test.

Those who wish to penetrate the barrier of birth and death must have this seal clearly verified before they may be let through. If you bring the "pumpkin seals" from various quarters to the pass of Heishan, they will be of no use at all.
Ascending the hall on the Mid-Autumn Festival, he said: "The mind is identical to the realm of empty space; one must simply maintain it with secret, clear wisdom.
The body manifests as the full moon disk; this is what Deva was able to discern. All say it demonstrates the essence of all Buddhas; all say it accords with the empty mind.
Yet in the end, it is like looking at a painted image, or like reaching for the moon by pointing at its finger. If you act in such a way, you are still within the gate of the Patriarchs."
Heaven and earth are vastly different. If you wish to bring joy and fulfillment to yourself, you must clearly understand the one upper orifice. Do you understand?
If you wish to recognize the shared root that transcends divergent views, know for certain that this very day is the Mid-Autumn Festival.

Ascending the hall, [the Master] raised an ancient precedent: Once there was a scholar who, while reading the *Sutra of the Names of Buddhas*, asked the Venerable Changsha Cen, "Of the hundreds of thousands of Buddhas, I have merely heard their names;
I do not yet know in which lands they dwell. Cen replied, "After Cui Hao inscribed his poem upon the Yellow Crane Tower, [Yang Jie could no longer ascend it]."
"Scholar, have you ever composed a verse? The scholar said, "I have not. Ceng said, "There is nothing better than composing one now.

The Master said, "At the point where the scholar questioned him, his clear faculty was right at his palm. Yet, although Changsha acted as he did for others, he could not avoid shifting his hands to shuttle the thread.
But tell me, ultimately, in what land do the hundreds of thousands of Buddhas dwell? Do you wish to see it?"
Listen to this verse from this mountain monk: Do not seek elsewhere for the sacred traces of the thousand Buddhas; The pivot of Changsha’s teaching has its own source.
If you wish to know where it is difficult to hide when face-to-face, It is right before the Yellow Crane Tower, on the Isle of Parrots.
Ascending the hall, he said: "The entire Tripitaka of the Buddhist teachings is upon your heads; the essential intent of the Patriarchs is at the soles of your feet.
There are certain practitioners of Zen who rely on intellectual understanding; when they hear this being said, they immediately claim it is like 'a hairless lock of chain shaking at both ends.
Yet look at this: throughout the twelve periods of the day, there is a hidden thing that constantly obstructs the breast. If you wish to..."
To penetrate this secure barrier, one must possess the eye upon the crown of the head. What is this eye upon the crowns of your heads?
After a long silence, he said: "A dot. Ascending the hall, he said:
"The auspicious snow falls from the void; the silver hare [the moon] emerges from the sea. Cao Shan perceives the extraordinary within the extraordinary; it is in the hands of Master Pang."

Illuminating the Mechanism. One person presents it directly and fully; another harmonizes with its subtle essence through the common path. If you can discern this, I grant that you possess the eye of discernment.
Truly, you may then repay the national grace. Should this not yet be so, I cannot help but reveal it layer upon layer. After a long silence, he said:
"Not only do plum buds burst forth before the spring, but there are also green pines to be seen amidst the snow."

He brought forth the Vajra Eye, which shone through and shattered a hundred thousand peaks piercing the heavens. The Master said, "Tell me, how was it when he returned to the West with his single shoe?
The monk said, "Leaves fall and return to their root; when coming, there were no words. The Master said, "You have only attained one peg."
The Master then said: "Tomorrow is the anniversary of the passing of the Great Monk Sīcin.

Furthermore, regarding the day when the patriarchs of the monastic communities throughout the world pass away, it is called a 'distant memorial. Since they have already awakened to the mind-ground, transcended the three realms, and suddenly leaped beyond birth and death, what is there to commemorate?
Yet, on this very day, the patch-robed monk reflects upon the passing of his own teacher."

Each person should contemplate in stillness: "Where is the 'Dead Heart' (Sīcitta) now? If one can realize this directly, one will see that the Dead Heart has never been extinguished from the very beginning.
Even if one performs Buddhist services with a single incense stick, a single flower, or various pure offerings, these may only be called preparatory practices (*prayoga*).
Only when one observes with diligent and tireless effort until a sudden awakening occurs does one not merely see the Dead Heart personally.

One also perceives the original face of all people. As for engaging in such preparatory practices and cultivation, is this merely to adorn the ground of the heart at the moment of death, or is it one's own meritorious cultivation?
If one perceives a self and an other, then two dharmas are established.
Once two dharmas are established, how can one avoid the affliction of birth and death? One should know that Master Sishin and...
All sentient and insentient beings are entirely one with Elder Heyshan;
Elder Heyshan and all sentient and insentient beings are entirely one with Master Siji. Have you not seen how this monk just now asked, "What is the meaning of the single shoe returned to the West?
Moreover, our late teacher Siji always delighted in citing the story of the single shoe returned to the West.
A discourse. [The Master] asked the assembly of monks: "Now, when the Dharma Master Baling entered parinirvāṇa, he repaid his former teacher with three turning words.
Today, Heyuan, while walking along, does not hesitate to swing his arms; he simply uses the story of the single sandal returning to the West to repay the virtue of his former teacher.
Furthermore, this story has been difficult to clarify throughout the ages, and various quarters have [offered different interpretations]."
This is called "hidden and manifest. Some say there cannot be two; others say that this alone is the one true reality.
If you think in such a way, you have not yet recognized the essential teaching of the Patriarch. Do you wish to see it? Clarity within turbidity, turbidity within clarity.
Do not say that the qilin has but a single horn. Traveling west toward the eastern road, the path is not mistaken. Great function is present at every turn.
Like a chick pecking and a hen pecking at the shell—*mo mo*. The profound essence and the vital mechanism are beyond calculation or conjecture.
Entering the hall, he raised the case of Chan Master Huìqīng of Bājiāo, who said: "At twenty-eight years of age, I traveled on pilgrimage to Mount Yǎng."
At the Southern Pagoda, [Baizhang] ascended the hall and said: "All of you here—if you were a true man, as soon as you emerged from your mother’s womb, you would let out a lion’s roar.
Can you roar? At these words, [his disciple] Xuefeng was able to find rest in body and mind, and he remained there for five years.
The Master said: "If Baizhang spoke in such a manner, could he truly bring about such rest? If it were so, it would be no different from a turtle that has not yet overturned."
It is always thus, whether on the mountain or otherwise; why wait until emerging from one’s mother’s womb to let out a lion’s roar?

Even Śākyamuni Tathāgata, before he had left his mother’s womb, had already completed the work of saving sentient beings. Yet, if you examine this closely, it still falls into the secondary level of teaching.
Do you all see it? After a long silence, he said: “Separated.”

Ascending the hall, the Master was asked by a novice monk for clarification on the "Four Critical Examinations" (Sì Liǎojiǎn). The Master provided these verses: "Seizing the person, not seizing the environment:
Where has Lingyun gone within the cave? The peach blossoms on the ridge bloom in profusion. "Seizing the environment, not seizing the person:
Having already seen the pivot of the Chéngyuán gate, One hears it first without even the need to strike the drum. "Both person and environment are seized: To know this thoroughly..."

Transcending the sages and surpassing the ordinary, this is precisely the moment of total gathering and total releasing. When person and environment are neither seized nor lost, things and self are both clearly and fully revealed;
body and mind are vividly present, inherently as they are. These four lines of verse sometimes "let go," such that throughout the ten directions, every single thing is manifest;
sometimes they "seize," such that within the boundless oceans of lands, where could one possibly find anything to grasp? If you...
When you have thus attained clarity, you may enter the marketplace and extend your hand; at the crossroads of the street, you can be certain that the Great Function will manifest before you.
If this is not yet the case, do not, by all means, mistake it for a mere human environment.
Ascending the hall, he said: "The First Mystery: before the skull is smashed through. The Second Mystery: illumination and function precede the occasion.
The Third Mystery: both object and self are fully present. The First Essential: within this, one must discern the omen. The Second Essential:

though the faculty may be sharp, it is not yet the wondrous. The Third Essential: facing it directly, one must turn the light back upon oneself. If, within a single phrase, one possesses clarity regarding these three..."
The three essentials of the profound mystery mean arriving directly at Heyang. If this is not yet so, then thirty years from now, every time you drink water, you will choke.
[The Master] descended from his seat.
Ascending the hall, he said: "For several days I have not entered the room; I shall now speak universally for you all regarding the maladies of Zen.
He then raised his whisk and asked, "Do you see it? If you see the whisk, you do not see the assembly; if you see the assembly, you do not see the whisk.
Therefore, throughout the entire world of the ten directions, everything is continuous and dense, truly without so much as a hair’s breadth of leakage. He then struck [the floor].
